newsitem.title: USA: U.S. consumer electronics sales seen rising 6 pct.
newsitem.headline: U.S. consumer electronics sales seen rising 6 pct.

text.p: U.S. sales of consumer electronics equipment, including television sets, videocassette recorders and stereos, are expected to increase by six percent this year, an industry trade group said on Thursday.
The Consumer Electronics Manufacturing Association (CEMA) said that 1997 sales are expected to rise to $69.5 billion from $65.7 billion last year.

The trade group made the forecast at the opening of its Winter Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas. The event will serve as a showcase for a host of new digital products, including cameras, cell phones and the long-awaited versatile disc player.

"1997 will be a solid year for the consumer electronics industry," Gary Shapiro, president of the trade group, said in a statement. "(It) will set the stage for two or more years of exceptional growth as more and more digital products enter the marketplace."
Shapiro said the combination of new products and falling prices for existing lines, including television sets, should boost sales in the year ahead.
Indeed, the trade group said it expected 27.6 million television sets to be purchased in the United States in 1997, even though more than 98 percent of U.S. households already own at least one set.

Many of the trade show's participants will focus on the new digital offerings. Among the most eagerly awaited are the introductions of digital versatile disc, or DVD, players by Philips Electronics NV and Sony Corp.

DVD equipment plays movies in much the same way as a videocassette recorder. But the technology is similar to an audio compact disc in size and shape. It holds movies in several different languages, plays on television sets or computers, and puts video in a digital format.
Though copyright issues have delayed the introduction of DVD players from their planned launch last autumn, industry professionals expect a resolution of those issues soon.
On Wednesday, Time Warner Inc's Warner Home Video unit said it would release 25 movies in DVD format this spring.
In an interview with Reuters, Warner Home Video President Warren Lieberfarb said the company intended to take a leading role as movie studios enter the DVD market.

He said Warner planned to release DVD titles at the same time as it issued them on videocassette and would price both formats comparatively. Movies set for release in March or April include "Batman", "Space Jam" and a director's cut version of "A Streetcar Named Desire."
